I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette:
David, a 52-year-old school principal, sought help after months of escalating distress following a violent assault eight months prior. He had been leaving a late-night meeting at the school, walking to his car, when he was ambushed from behind. The attack itself was a blur of sudden force and terrifying helplessness, leaving him with a concussion and a profound sense of vulnerability.

In the aftermath, David found that trying to deliberately remember the details of what happened was remarkably difficult; it was as if a crucial part of the narrative was locked away, frustrating his attempts to make sense of it. Yet, paradoxically, his memories of the frightening event were like a film that would play over and over in his mind, unsolicited and vivid. These intrusive replays were not just mental images; when these memories came to mind, he felt his body was in the same contorted position as when the frightening event occurred, a visceral reenactment that left him physically shaken.

It was these intrusive, bodily memories that began to profoundly shape his present experience. As these fragmented, vivid replays of the assault would spontaneously surface, they would immediately ignite his threat system. Suddenly, David would feel jumpy and easily startled by unexpected noises or movements in the usually bustling school hallways. This heightened internal state quickly translated into a constant, external vigilance. Now, as soon as he entered any room or building, whether it was the school gymnasium for an assembly or a parent-teacher conference in a classroom, he found himself instinctively scanning for exits, his eyes darting to locate the quickest escape route. What frightened him most was the pervasive sense that danger lurked everywhere, leading him to notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment – a heavy stapler on a desk, a fire extinguisher on the wall, even a pair of scissors left out in a craft room – seeing them not as tools, but as potential instruments of harm.

This constant hypervigilance made his job as a principal increasingly arduous. During a staff meeting, while trying to lead a discussion on curriculum changes, a sudden clatter from the cafeteria next door would send a jolt through him, making him visibly flinch. He found himself constantly distracted, his attention split between the conversation at hand and his internal scan of the room for threats. The difficulty he experienced trying to deliberately recall the event also contributed to a nagging feeling of confusion, making it harder to process his experience. He began to withdraw, avoiding opportunities to mingle with parents or attend community events, fearing the unpredictable nature of crowds and unfamiliar spaces. His wife, Maria, noticed his increasing agitation and the way he would jump at the slightest sound at home. David knew he couldn't continue this way. The tightening grip of his past trauma on his daily life, particularly the way his own memories were turning his world into a landscape of constant threat, was what finally prompted him to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the calm authority he once embodied for his students and staff.
